Predictable GRPO: A Closed-Form Model of Training Dynamics

Rajat Ghosh rajat.ghosh11@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: San Jose, USA    Datta Nimmaturi venkatadattasainimmaturi@gmail.com ††thanks: Datta Nimmaturi contributed to the preliminary ideation and early validation while working at Nutanix. Affiliation: Unsloth Affiliation: Hyderabad, India    Aryan Singhal aryan.singhal2001@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: San Jose, USA    Vaishnavi Bhargava vaishnavi.bhargava2605@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: San Jose, USA    Henry Wong henrylwongx@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: San Jose, USA    Johnu George johnugeorge109@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: Bengaluru, India    Debojyoti Dutta ddutta@gmail.com Affiliation: Nutanix Affiliation: San Jose, USA
Abstract

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become a standard tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, yet its training dynamics are still described empirically: reward trajectories are fit with low-parameter functional forms whose constants carry no mechanistic meaning, and hyperparameter choices remain a matter of trial and error. We develop a first-principles reduced-order model of these dynamics. Under a single mean-field assumption that summarizes the policy by its expected reward, we reduce the GRPO update to a stochastically-forced damped oscillator whose mass, damping, and stiffness are fixed in closed form by the optimizer hyperparameters together with a single measured curvature scale—momentum supplies the inertia, off-policy lag erodes the damping, and the group size enters only as a noise temperature. The reduction has three consequences. First, it subsumes the empirical single-exponential saturation law as its overdamped limit, recasting the fitted plateau, timescale, and size exponent as the fixed point, inverse stiffness, and curvature-scaling exponent of the underlying potential, and adding, through the retained inertial term, the slow-start phase the single exponential cannot represent. Second, it yields predictions tied to independently measurable quantities rather than fitted ones: group-size invariance of the deterministic trajectory with a 1/G1/G stationary fluctuation, a sharp stability threshold in the refresh interval, and an overdamped-to-oscillatory transition. Third, it furnishes diagnostics that separate failure modes a reward curve alone conflates—reward hacking, advantage degeneracy, policy concentration, and dynamical instability. Across three models and two group sizes, the closed-form trajectory fits training reward to R2≥0.91R^{2}\geq 0.91 and the predicted group-size invariance holds on both the reward curve and out-of-distribution transfer to eight math benchmarks. The stability and oscillatory predictions are exercised in a controlled exact-reduction setting where the mean-field assumption holds exactly: a softmax-bandit reduction reproduces the predicted overdamped-to-oscillatory transition and locates the refresh-interval stability threshold at the independently measured stiffness, with a deep-network demonstration left to future work.

GRPO, Predictability

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities after RL post-training (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), yet the mechanisms by which they acquire these capabilities remain largely opaque (Yue et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026). Scaling RL compute is a critical paradigm for advancing LLM capability frontier. For instance, Deepseek-R1-Zero used 100,000 H800 GPU hours for RL post-training—3.75% of its pre-training compute (Guo et al., 2025). Moreover, the trend in RL post-training compute is amplified in frontier LLMs—more than 10×\times increase from o1 to o3 (OpenAI, 2025) and a similar jump from Grok-3 to Grok-4 (xAI, 2025).

While RL compute scale massively, the general understanding of the field has remained more art than science. Recent breakthroughs in RL compute are generally driven by a handful of frontier labs in the form of novel algorithms (Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025) and training reports (MiniMax et al., 2025; Mistral-AI et al., 2025). These studies provide specific solutions but lack scientific understanding of RL compute scaling in general. This leads to perpetual trial-and-error mode in RL post-training which is both sub-optimal and cost-prohibitive. Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    A reduced-order model of GRPO training. Under a single mean-field assumption (Assumption 1), we reduce the GRPO update (3) to a stochastically-forced damped oscillator (Theorem 7) whose coefficients Meff,Ceff,KeffM_{\mathrm{eff}},C_{\mathrm{eff}},K_{\mathrm{eff}} are given in closed form (9). The reduction is mechanical apart from this assumption and a controlled second-order truncation in the step size and refresh lag: momentum promotes the gradient flow to second order (Lemma 4), off-policy lag supplies inertia while eroding damping (Lemma 5), and the group size enters as a noise temperature (Lemma 6).

  2. 2.

    A mechanistic account of the empirical saturation law. We show that the single-exponential reward law (13) fitted in prior work is the overdamped limit of our model (Corollary 13), which reinterprets its plateau, timescale, and size exponent as the fixed point, inverse stiffness, and curvature-scaling exponent of the dynamics rather than as fitted constants (15). Retaining the inertial term yields the slow-start inflection that the single-exponential form cannot represent (Proposition 14).

  3. 3.

    Falsifiable predictions pinned to measurable quantities. Because the coefficients are tied to independently observable slopes, the model yields predictions rather than fits: group-size invariance of the deterministic trajectory with a 1/G1/G stationary fluctuation (Proposition 10), a sharp stability threshold K​η​Kref>1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}>1-\mu (Proposition 9), and an overdamped-to-oscillatory transition under refresh-interval sweeps (Section 3.5).

  4. 4.

    Diagnostics that separate distinct failure modes. We operationalize the model as four read-outs that a reward curve alone cannot disentangle—train–eval decoupling, advantage degeneracy, policy concentration, and dynamical instability—thereby distinguishing erosion of the mean-field premise (Assumption 1) from loss of stability of the dynamics (Theorem 7).

  5. 5.

    Empirical validation. Across three models and two group sizes, the three-phase law (16) fits the training-reward trajectories with R2≥0.91R^{2}\geq 0.91, and the predicted group-size invariance of Proposition 10 is borne out on both the mean trajectory and out-of-distribution transfer to eight benchmarks. The stability and oscillatory predictions, untestable on the overdamped GSM8K runs, are instead exercised in a controlled exact-reduction setting (Section 5.6): a softmax-bandit reduction in which Assumption 1 holds exactly reproduces the overdamped-to-oscillatory transition and pins the refresh-interval threshold of Proposition 9 at the independently measured stiffness, leaving the deep-network demonstration to future work.

2 Related Work

Theory of GRPO and RLVR.

A growing line of work seeks to explain why reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, rather than merely demonstrating that it does. Mroueh (2025) characterizes the effective loss of GRPO and establishes the “success amplification” property—the existence of a stable fixed point whose expected reward exceeds that of the reference policy—together with a one-step contraction governing the approach to it. Vojnovic and Yun (2025) analyze the alignment objective induced by GRPO and identify a β​σ​(πθ)\beta\sigma(\pi_{\theta}) effective-regularization form for the KL-anchored term. We take both results as inputs rather than re-deriving them: Assumption 1 imports the fixed point p⋆p^{\star} and the contraction h′​(p⋆)h^{\prime}(p^{\star}) from Mroueh (2025), and Lemma 3 inherits the stiffness scale from the effective-regularization form of Vojnovic and Yun (2025). A separate strand asks whether RLVR confers new capabilities or sharpens existing ones (Yue et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026); this question is orthogonal to ours, which concerns the trajectory along which a fixed reward signal is optimized rather than the source of the reward itself.

Empirical scaling and saturation laws.

A complementary body of work fits GRPO reward trajectories with low-parameter functional forms. Nimmaturi et al. (2025) propose predictive scaling laws for GRPO training, and Ghosh et al. (2026) report that across model families and scales the reward follows the saturating law of (13), with a size-dependent timescale M0.3M^{0.3}. These laws are accurate and useful for compute planning, but their parameters are fitted constants without mechanistic referents: the plateau, the timescale, and the size exponent are read off the data rather than predicted. Our reduction subsumes this line of work rather than competing with it. Corollary 13 shows that the single-exponential law (13) is precisely the overdamped limit of Theorem 7, and Equation (15) reinterprets the M0.3M^{0.3} exponent as a curvature-scaling exponent of the underlying potential. Where the inertial term is retained, Proposition 14 further predicts the slow-start phase that the single exponential cannot represent, recovering the full three-phase shape these fits leave unexplained.

Algorithms and training reports.

Much of the recent progress in RL post-training arrives as novel algorithms (Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025) and large-scale training reports (MiniMax et al., 2025; Mistral-AI et al., 2025). These contributions advance the practical frontier and report specific, hard-won configurations, but they are not designed to yield a general account of how a training curve depends on its hyperparameters; the prescriptions they offer are calibrated to a particular setting and do not, on their own, predict behavior outside it. Our aim is complementary: rather than a new optimizer or a new run, we provide a closed-form relationship between the training configuration (β,η,μ,G,Kref)(\beta,\eta,\mu,G,K_{\mathrm{ref}}) and the resulting trajectory, with the group-size invariance of Proposition 10 and the stability threshold of Proposition 9 as falsifiable consequences.

Positioning.

The boundary of our contribution is therefore sharp. We import the fixed point and contraction from Mroueh (2025) and the regularization scale from Vojnovic and Yun (2025); what is new is the promotion of the resulting first-order relaxation to a second-order system, with the inertia and damping supplied mechanically by momentum (Lemma 4) and off-policy lag (Lemma 5), and the consequent subsumption of the empirical saturation laws (Nimmaturi et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2026) as the overdamped limit of a single equation. The reduction is conditional on the mean-field assumption (Remark 12) and is not an unconditional account of GRPO; it is, rather, the minimal dynamical model that turns fitted reward curves into derived ones.

3 Formalism

3.1 Setup

For a prompt qq, GRPO samples a group of GG completions {oi}i=1G∼πθold(⋅∣q)\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid q), scores them with a reward ri=R⁡(q,oi)r_{i}=R(q,o_{i}), and forms the group-relative advantage

Ai=ri−r¯std⁡(r),r¯=1G​∑jrj.A_{i}\;=\;\frac{r_{i}-\bar{r}}{\std(r)},\qquad\bar{r}=\tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_{j}r_{j}. (1)

The (unclipped) objective, with KL anchoring weight β>0\beta>0 to a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, is

J(θ)=𝔼q𝔼{oi}∼πθold[1G∑i=1Gπθ​(oi∣q)πθold​(oi∣q)Ai]−β𝔼q[DKL(πθ∥πref)].J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q}\,\mathbb{E}_{\{o_{i}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}\mid q)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{i}\mid q)}\,A_{i}\right]-\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)\right]. (2)

Parameters are updated by stochastic ascent with learning rate η\eta and momentum coefficient μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) (the role played by Adam’s β1\beta_{1}), and the sampling policy is refreshed every KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} steps:

θk+1=θk+η​∇J^​(θk,θold)+μ⁡(θk−θk−1),θold=θk−Kref.\theta_{k+1}=\theta_{k}+\eta\,\widehat{\nabla J}(\theta_{k};\theta_{\mathrm{old}})+\mu\,(\theta_{k}-\theta_{k-1}),\qquad\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=\theta_{k-K_{\mathrm{ref}}}. (3)

We use δ\delta for the step-to-time conversion. The discrete map (3) is the object of interest; the continuous-time equations below are its modified equation, tracking the iteration to O⁡(δ2)O(\delta^{2}) in the sense of backward-error analysis. Setting δ=1\delta=1 in final expressions then merely fixes the time unit as one optimizer step, so the effective coefficients are measured in step-units.

3.2 The mean-field reduction

Assumption 1 (Scalar order parameter).

Let p​(θ)=𝔼o∼πθ​[R]p(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{o\sim\pi_{\theta}}[R] denote the expected reward. There exists a C2C^{2} drift g:[0,1]→ℝg:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} such that the gradient-flow projection of (3) satisfies p˙=g⁡(p)+o⁡(1)\dot{p}=g(p)+o(1) as δ→0\delta\to 0, and the dynamics of θ\theta are summarized by pp to leading order. Moreover gg admits a unique stable fixed point p⋆∈(pref,1)p^{\star}\in(p_{\mathrm{ref}},1), with one-step contraction h′​(p⋆)=1+δ​g′​(p⋆)∈(−1,1)h^{\prime}(p^{\star})=1+\delta\,g^{\prime}(p^{\star})\in(-1,1).

Assumption 1 is the only non-mechanical step in what follows. It holds exactly for tabular/softmax parameterizations and is an approximation for deep networks. The existence of p⋆p^{\star} in the interior above prefp_{\mathrm{ref}} (the “success amplification” property) and the value of the contraction h′​(p⋆)h^{\prime}(p^{\star}) are taken from Mroueh (2025); we do not re-derive them.

Lemma 6 (Group size is a temperature).

The minibatch estimator satisfies ∇J^=∇J+G−1/2ζk\widehat{\nabla J}=\nabla J+G^{-1/2}\zeta_{k} with ζk\zeta_{k} zero-mean and Cov⁡(ζk)∝σadv2\operatorname{Cov}(\zeta_{k})\propto\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}}^{2}. Proposition 10 (Group-size invariance of the deterministic dynamics).

The fixed point p⋆p^{\star} and the deterministic coefficients (9) are independent of GG; GG enters (8) only through the forcing. Consequently, in the stable regime K​η​Kref<1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}<1-\mu of Proposition 9, the stationary fluctuation of the order parameter obeys

⟨e2⟩∞∝DG​Ceff​Keff∝1G,\langle e^{2}\rangle_{\infty}\;\propto\;\frac{D}{G\,C_{\mathrm{eff}}\,K_{\mathrm{eff}}}\;\propto\;\frac{1}{G}, (12)

Proof.

Hence ⟨e2⟩∞∝1/G\langle e^{2}\rangle_{\infty}\propto 1/G and the deterministic part is GG-free. ∎

Remark 11 (Empirical correspondences).

Proposition 8 predicts that runs with small learning rate, no momentum, and frequent refresh are overdamped and exhibit monotone saturation to p⋆p^{\star}, matching the regime in which a first-order fixed-point fit attains high R2R^{2}. Proposition 9 predicts divergence past a sharp refresh-interval threshold, consistent with the instability of stale-policy training. Proposition 10 predicts that reducing GG leaves the mean trajectory intact and raises only the variance, consistent with reports that two rollouts per prompt match sixteen up to noise.

Remark 12 (Scope).

Theorem 7 rests on two modeling steps, not one. The first is Assumption 1, the mean-field reduction to a scalar order parameter; the second is the backward-error (modified-equation) expansion of Lemmas 4 and 5, truncated at second order in the step size δ\delta and the refresh lag τ\tau, which drops O⁡(δ3,τ3)O(\delta^{3},\tau^{3}) terms and is therefore accurate only for small δ\delta and τ\tau. Within that truncation the algebra of Lemmas 2–6 is exact (verified symbolically; see Appendix A), and Section 5.6 quantifies the truncation error directly against the exact dynamics. The coefficients are moreover local linearizations at p⋆p^{\star}, so (8) describes the approach to the fixed point rather than global dynamics, and the curvature KK is identifiable from the early-training slope λ=K/c\lambda=K/c rather than predicted. The appropriate reading is a reduced-order model conditional on the mean-field reduction and the small-step expansion, not an unconditional account of GRPO.

3.5 The empirical reward-saturation law as an overdamped limit

The reduced-order equation (8) makes contact with empirical work that fits GRPO reward trajectories with simple parametric forms (Nimmaturi et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2026). In particular, Ghosh et al. (2026) report that across model families and scales the reward follows the saturating law

R(t,M)=R∞(1−e−t/M0.3),R(t,M)=R_{\infty}\bigl(1-e^{-t/M^{0.3}}\bigr), (13)

with a steady-state reward R∞R_{\infty} that grows with model size MM and a single size-dependent timescale M0.3M^{0.3}. We show that (13) is the overdamped limit of Theorem 7, and that retaining the inertial term resolves the early “slow-start” phase that (13) cannot represent.

Throughout we identify reward with the order parameter, R≡pR\equiv p, write R∞≡p⋆R_{\infty}\equiv p^{\star} for the plateau, and take the trajectory to start from rest, p˙​(0)=0\dot{p}(0)=0, at initial reward R0R_{0}. By Proposition 10 the forcing sets only the stationary fluctuation, so the mean trajectory obeys the deterministic part of (8).

Corollary 13 (Saturation law).

In the overdamped regime ζ≥1\zeta\geq 1, the mean reward of Theorem 7 is

R⁡(t)=R∞−(R∞−R0)​e−λ​t,λ=KeffCeff,R(t)=R_{\infty}-(R_{\infty}-R_{0})\,e^{-\lambda t},\qquad\lambda=\frac{K_{\mathrm{eff}}}{C_{\mathrm{eff}}}, (14)

and, when R0≪R∞R_{0}\ll R_{\infty}, reduces to the empirical form (13) with timescale τ=1/λ=Ceff/Keff=[(1−μ)−K​η​Kref]/(η​K)\tau=1/\lambda=C_{\mathrm{eff}}/K_{\mathrm{eff}}=\bigl[(1-\mu)-K\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr]/(\eta K).

Proof.

When ζ≫1\zeta\gg 1 the two roots of (8) separate (Proposition 8); after the fast mode decays the slow pole −Keff/Ceff-K_{\mathrm{eff}}/C_{\mathrm{eff}} governs, so e⁡(t)=e⁡(0)​e−λ​te(t)=e(0)\,e^{-\lambda t} with e=R−R∞e=R-R_{\infty}. Substituting e⁡(0)=R0−R∞e(0)=R_{0}-R_{\infty} gives (14); dropping the R0/R∞R_{0}/R_{\infty} term gives (13). ∎

Corollary 13 supplies mechanistic content for the three quantities in (13). The plateau is the GRPO fixed point, R∞=p⋆​(M)R_{\infty}=p^{\star}(M), so its growth with scale is the success amplification of Mroueh (2025) rather than a fitted constant. The timescale is an inverse stiffness, τ=1/(η​K)\tau=1/(\eta K) at μ=Kref=0\mu=K_{\mathrm{ref}}=0, so the empirical exponent is a curvature-scaling exponent,

τ∝M0.3⟺K⁡(M)∝η−1​M−0.3:\tau\propto M^{0.3}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;K(M)\propto\eta^{-1}M^{-0.3}: (15)

a larger model approaches a higher fixed point along a flatter potential, consistent with lazy/NTK-regime slowdown. Finally, the initial reward R0R_{0} enters (14) as the amplitude and is absent from (13) only through the approximation R0≪R∞R_{0}\ll R_{\infty}.

Proposition 14 (Three-phase refinement).

Retaining the inertial term, the critically-damped (ζ=1\zeta=1) mean trajectory from rest is

R⁡(t)R∞=1−(1+ωn​t)​e−ωn​t,ωn=Keff/Meff,\frac{R(t)}{R_{\infty}}=1-\bigl(1+\omega_{n}t\bigr)e^{-\omega_{n}t},\qquad\omega_{n}=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{eff}}/M_{\mathrm{eff}}}, (16)

which satisfies R′​(0)=0R^{\prime}(0)=0 and has an inflection at t⋆=1/ωnt^{\star}=1/\omega_{n}. The general overdamped case replaces (16) by the two-exponential response with poles s1,2=−ωn​(ζ∓ζ2−1)s_{1,2}=-\omega_{n}\bigl(\zeta\mp\sqrt{\zeta^{2}-1}\bigr).

Proof.

The step response of (8) from rest at ζ=1\zeta=1 has the repeated pole −ωn-\omega_{n}, yielding (16). Differentiating, R′​(t)=R∞​ωn2​t​e−ωn​tR^{\prime}(t)=R_{\infty}\,\omega_{n}^{2}\,t\,e^{-\omega_{n}t}, so R′​(0)=0R^{\prime}(0)=0 and R′′​(t⋆)=0R^{\prime\prime}(t^{\star})=0 at t⋆=1/ωnt^{\star}=1/\omega_{n}. ∎

Equation (16) reproduces the full three-phase trajectory reported by Ghosh et al. (2026)—a slow start (R′​(0)=0R^{\prime}(0)=0), a rapid phase centered at the inflection t⋆=1/ωnt^{\star}=1/\omega_{n}, and a plateau—whereas the single exponential (13) is concave with maximal slope at t=0t=0 and so has no slow-start phase. The inertia responsible for the inflection is exactly the momentum-plus-lag mass MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}} of Lemma 5. For empirical practice this implies that the quantity expected to collapse across scales is not R/R∞R/R_{\infty} but the doubly normalized deviation

R⁡(t)−R0R∞−R0=1−(1+ωn​t)​e−ωn​t,\frac{R(t)-R_{0}}{R_{\infty}-R_{0}}=1-(1+\omega_{n}t)\,e^{-\omega_{n}t}, (17)

which removes both the reward scale and the initial offset.

3.6 A falsifiable prediction

Fix (β,η,μ,G)(\beta,\eta,\mu,G) and sweep the refresh interval KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}}. Equation (10) predicts a monotone-to-oscillatory transition in the learning curve at ζ=1\zeta=1, and divergence at the threshold (11); both critical values are pinned by the independently measurable slope KK. We test this prediction directly in Section 5.6, in an exact softmax reduction where Assumption 1 holds without approximation.

4 Experimental Setup

This section describes the experimental protocol used to test the reduced-order model of Section 3. The design follows directly from what the theory asks of the data. Theorem 7 predicts a specific closed-form trajectory toward a fixed point, so we need reward curves logged densely enough to fit a three-parameter law; Proposition 10 predicts that the deterministic trajectory is invariant to the group size GG while the stationary fluctuation scales as 1/G1/G, so we run every configuration at two group sizes; and the four diagnostics of Section 1 read out internal training quantities—advantage spread, entropy, KL, gradient norm, and the importance-sampling ratio—so we log each of them at every step rather than only the scalar reward.

4.1 Models

We study three open-weight models chosen to span the regimes in which Assumption 1 is expected to hold to differing degrees:

  • •

    Nemotron-Mini-4B (NVIDIA, 2024), a 44B general-purpose instruction-tuned model;

  • •

    DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), a 77B chat model, the largest in our study and the one without explicit reasoning distillation;

  • •

    DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (Guo et al., 2025), a 1.51.5B model distilled from R1 reasoning traces and therefore the only reasoning-specialized model of the three.

The spread in scale (1.51.5B–77B) and in reasoning specialization lets us separate effects of the dynamics from effects of the base capability: the reasoning-distilled model is the one for which the scalar order-parameter reduction is expected to remain cleanest, a prediction we test directly through the policy-concentration diagnostic of Section 5.1 onward.

4.2 Training Setup

All three models are post-trained with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) on the GSM8K training split (Cobbe et al., 2021) of grade-school word problems, using a binary verifiable reward that checks the parsed final answer against the gold solution. Training uses parameter-efficient LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) (rank r=16r=16, α=64\alpha=64, dropout 0.050.05) applied to the query, key, value, output, and MLP up/down/gate projections, with the adapters merged into the base weights for evaluation. The full configuration is given in Table 2 (Appendix B); the settings most relevant to the theory are the learning rate η=1×10−5\eta=1\times 10^{-5}, the KL anchoring weight β=0.005\beta=0.005, the clipping coefficient ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2, the sampling temperature 0.80.8, and a training horizon of two epochs. The small learning rate is deliberate: by Proposition 8 it places the product K​η​KrefK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}} well below 1−μ1-\mu, so every run is expected to sit in the overdamped regime where the closed-form saturation law of Corollary 13 applies. Probing the under-damped and unstable regimes of Propositions 9–14 would require raising η\eta or the refresh interval KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}}, which we leave to future work.

Group sizes and seeds.

The central manipulation is the GRPO group size, the number of completions GG sampled per prompt to form the group-relative advantage of Eq. (1). We run every model at G∈{4,16}G\in\{4,16\}, a fourfold change in rollout budget, so that the group-size invariance of Proposition 10 can be tested as a controlled comparison. To separate the deterministic trajectory from run-to-run noise—the 1/G1/G stationary fluctuation that the theory attributes to the forcing term—each configuration is run over two random seeds {42,3407}\{42,3407\}, and all reported curves are seed-averaged with ±\pm one standard deviation bands.

Logged quantities.

Beyond the training and held-out reward, we log at each optimizer step the quantities required by the four diagnostics: the within-group reward standard deviation σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} (train/reward_std), the collapsed-prompt fraction (train/frac_reward_zero_std), the token-level policy entropy (train/entropy), the KL to the reference (train/kl), the gradient norm (train/grad_norm), and the maximum importance-sampling ratio (train/sampling/importance_sampling_ratio/max). These are the empirical witnesses for, respectively, the noise temperature of Lemma 6, the advantage degeneracy that breaks Eq. (1), the scalar-reduction premise of Assumption 1, and the off-policy lag and stability threshold of Lemma 5 and Proposition 9.

4.3 Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate along two axes. In-distribution, we track the held-out GSM8K reward and accuracy logged every 100100 steps, which provide the eval-side trajectories used both for the three-phase fit and for the reward-hacking (train–eval co-saturation) diagnostic. Out-of-distribution, we measure zero-shot transfer of the GSM8K-trained policies—without any further tuning—to eight external math benchmarks spanning the full difficulty range, from grade-school word problems to olympiad competition mathematics: GSM-Plus (Li et al., 2024), MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024), OpenMath2 (Toshniwal et al., 2024), NuminaMath (Jia et al., 2024), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), IMO-Bench, AIME-2026, and HMMT-2025. The benchmarks are ordered, roughly, by distance from the GSM8K training distribution, which lets us read transfer as a function of that distance.

Metric.

Transfer is reported as pass@kk for k∈{1,5}k\in\{1,5\}, the fraction of problems solved within kk sampled completions, as mean ±\pm standard deviation over seeds. Reporting both k=1k=1 and k=5k=5 guards against mistaking a temperature-induced broadening of the output distribution for a genuine accuracy gain: an improvement that reflects real capability raises pass@1 and not merely pass@5. For the larger benchmarks we subsample for tractability—20002000 examples each from MetaMathQA and OpenMath2—and for NuminaMath we skip the single proof problem that is not objectively verifiable; benchmark sizes are noted in Table 1.

4.4 Curve-Fitting Methodology

To test the closed-form prediction of Theorem 7 we fit each seed-averaged trajectory with the critically-damped three-phase law of Proposition 14,

R⁡(t)=R∞−(R∞−R0)​(1+ωn​t)​e−ωn​t,R(t)\;=\;R_{\infty}-(R_{\infty}-R_{0})\,(1+\omega_{n}t)\,e^{-\omega_{n}t},

a three-parameter family in the initial reward R0R_{0}, the plateau R∞=p⋆R_{\infty}=p^{\star}, and the natural frequency ωn=Keff/Meff\omega_{n}=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{eff}}/M_{\mathrm{eff}}}. Fits are obtained by nonlinear least squares against the seed-averaged curve, and goodness of fit is reported as the in-panel coefficient of determination R2R^{2} measured on that curve. The same fitted (R0,R∞)(R_{0},R_{\infty}) are reused to form the scale- and offset-free progress variable u⁡(t)=(R⁡(t)−R0)/(R∞−R0)u(t)=(R(t)-R_{0})/(R_{\infty}-R_{0}) that underlies the doubly-normalized co-saturation diagnostic. Because the deterministic coefficients are GG-independent by Proposition 10, a single functional form is fit to both group sizes, and agreement of the fitted R∞R_{\infty} and shape across G∈{4,16}G\in\{4,16\} is itself one of the predictions under test.

5 Results

5.1 Description of GRPO Training Dynamics

We train three models—Nemotron-Mini-4B, DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B—with GRPO on GSM8K under two group sizes G∈{4,16}G\in\{4,16\}, using the configuration of Table 2 in Appendix and averaging over seeds {42,3407}\{42,3407\}. For each run we log the training reward, the held-out evaluation reward, and the evaluation accuracy as functions of the optimizer step, and we fit each trajectory with the critically-damped three-phase law of Proposition 14,

R⁡(t)=R∞−(R∞−R0)​(1+ωn​t)​e−ωn​t,R(t)\;=\;R_{\infty}-(R_{\infty}-R_{0})\,(1+\omega_{n}t)\,e^{-\omega_{n}t},

a three-parameter family in (R0,R∞,ωn)(R_{0},R_{\infty},\omega_{n}). Figure 1 collects the resulting curves with the in-panel coefficients of determination.

The central observation is that the training-reward trajectories are captured by the reduced-order model to high accuracy: across all three models and both group sizes the fit attains R2≥0.91R^{2}\geq 0.91 (panels (a)–(f)), reaching R2=0.97R^{2}=0.97 for the Nemotron and Qwen-1.5B runs. The three regimes predicted by Eq. 17 are visible in every train panel: (i) a slow start in which the reward changes little—the signature of the zero-velocity initial condition R′​(0)=0R^{\prime}(0)=0 enforced by the momentum-plus-lag mass MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}} of Lemma 5; (ii) a rapid phase centered on the inflection t⋆=1/ωnt^{\star}=1/\omega_{n}; and (iii) a plateau at R∞=p⋆R_{\infty}=p^{\star}, the GRPO fixed point of Assumption 1. The single-exponential saturation law in Eq. 13, being concave from t=0t=0 with maximal initial slope, cannot represent the slow start; it is precisely the retained inertia that supplies the early inflection and lifts the fit to the observed quality.

Increasing GG from 44 to 1616 leaves the fitted plateau R∞R_{\infty} and the qualitative slow-start/rapid-phase/plateau shape essentially unchanged while visibly narrowing the run-to-run scatter (the shaded ±\pms.d. band contracts at G=16G=16). This is the empirical content of the deterministic GG-invariance of the coefficients Eq. 10: GG enters the dynamics only through the forcing intensity D/GD/G, so it sets the stationary fluctuation⟨e2⟩∞∝1/G\langle e^{2}\rangle_{\infty}\propto 1/G rather than the mean trajectory. The two rollout budgets therefore trace the same mean curve at different noise levels, consistent with reports that two rollouts per prompt match sixteen up to noise.

The evaluation-side metrics are more nuanced. At G=16G=16 the held-out reward is fit well (panels (j)–(l), R2R^{2} from 0.920.92 to 0.980.98) and the evaluation accuracy improves substantially (panels (p)–(r), R2R^{2} from 0.750.75 to 0.950.95), confirming that the train-time order parameter p=𝔼⁡[R]p=\mathbb{E}[R] tracks the held-out quantities through saturation. At G=4G=4, by contrast, the eval-reward and eval-accuracy fits degrade markedly (panels (g)–(i) and (m)–(n), R2≈0.55R^{2}\approx 0.55–0.690.69). We read this as a logging artifact rather than a breakdown of the dynamics: evaluation is recorded only every 100100 steps (Table 2 in Appendix), and at the smaller group size the seed-averaged eval curve is both shorter and noisier, leaving too few points to pin a three-parameter fit. The G=16G=16 panels, which span more steps and average over more rollouts per step, recover the fit on the same quantities. The lone exception at G=4G=4 is Qwen-1.5B, whose eval-accuracy fit is already high (R2=0.97R^{2}=0.97, panel (o))—the model that also shows the cleanest reward–eval coupling in our diagnostics.

Taken together, Figure 1 substantiates the empirical claim of Section 3: within the stable, mean-field regime, GRPO reward trajectories are not merely monotone but follow the specific closed-form shape of an overdamped-to-critically-damped second-order relaxation toward a fixed point, with the deterministic part of that shape independent of group size.

5.2 Reward Hacking Investigation

Reward hacking is the regime in which the optimizer continues to drive the training reward toward its plateau while the held-out objective fails to follow: the policy games features of the training signal that do not transfer. If the train and eval rewards both track the same scalar order parameter p=𝔼⁡[R]p=\mathbb{E}[R] relaxing to R∞=p⋆R_{\infty}=p^{\star}, then by the saturation law (Eq. 14) each obeys −log⁡(R∞−R⁡(t))=λ​t−log⁡(R∞−R0)-\log\!\bigl(R_{\infty}-R(t)\bigr)=\lambda t-\log(R_{\infty}-R_{0}), a line whose slope is the shared relaxation rate λ\lambda. A healthy run is therefore one in which train and eval co-saturate—same shape, same rate—and reward hacking is the failure of that co-saturation. Figure 2 makes this operational through two complementary read-outs.

Doubly-normalized plateau ratio (row 1).

For each metric we form the scale- and offset-free progress variable u⁡(t)=(R⁡(t)−R0)/(R∞−R0)u(t)=\bigl(R(t)-R_{0}\bigr)/\bigl(R_{\infty}-R_{0}\bigr) using the fitted (R0,R∞)(R_{0},R_{\infty}) of Proposition 14, and plot ueval​(t)u_{\mathrm{eval}}(t) against utrain​(t)u_{\mathrm{train}}(t) parametrically (panels (a)–(c), star at the final step). The normalization removes the reward scale and the initial offset, so a run that co-saturates falls on the diagonal reference y=xy=x, regardless of how fast it trains or how high its plateau sits. A run whose eval progress lags its train progress—reward rising on the training distribution faster than it generalizes—bends below the diagonal, and the vertical gap at a given utrainu_{\mathrm{train}} is a direct, parameter-free measure of the hacking deficit.

Rolling coupling ratio (row 2).

The parametric view summarizes the whole run but obscures when decoupling sets in. We therefore estimate the local rates by regressing −log⁡(R∞−R⁡(t))-\log\!\bigl(R_{\infty}-R(t)\bigr) on the step within a rolling window (45% of the eval-step span), separately for the train and eval points, and report their ratio

ρ⁡(t)=λeval​(t)|λtrain​(t)|.\rho(t)=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{eval}}(t)}{\lvert\lambda_{\mathrm{train}}(t)\rvert}.

Co-saturation is ρ≈1\rho\approx 1; the hacking signature is ρ→0\rho\to 0, the eval rate collapsing relative to the train rate. We plot ρ\rho on a symmetric-log axis (linthresh=1\mathrm{linthresh}=1) against training progress normalized per GG, so the G=4G=4 and G=16G=16 traces overlay and the healthy band near unity renders linearly.

Findings.

Three patterns emerge. (i) At G=4G=4, Nemotron-Mini-4B and DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat both display the hacking signature in both read-outs: their parametric curves (panels (a),(b)) sit well below the diagonal, and the coupling ratio (panels (d),(e)) stays below one throughout training, so the held-out reward never matches the pace of the training reward. (ii) DeepSeek-R1-Distill- Qwen-1.5B at G=16G=16 (panel (f), purple) is the cleanest healthy run, with ρ≈1\rho\approx 1 over the middle 80%80\% of training; its parametric curve correspondingly hugs the diagonal. This is consistent with Section 5.1, where Qwen-1.5B was the one model whose eval-accuracy trajectory was already well described by the reduced-order fit at G=4G=4 (panel (o) of Figure 1): the cleanest order-parameter coupling here and the cleanest fit there are the same phenomenon. (iii) The two read-outs agree on the direction of the group-size effect—larger GG pushes runs toward the diagonal and ρ\rho toward unity—so the rollout budget that Proposition 10 predicts to leave the mean train trajectory unchanged nonetheless improves the train–eval coupling, an effect outside the scalar reduction and attributable to the reduced gradient noise at larger GG.

One reading caveat accompanies the coupling ratio. Late in training, as Rtrain→R∞R_{\mathrm{train}}\to R_{\infty}, the train rate λtrain→0\lambda_{\mathrm{train}}\to 0 and ρ\rho becomes ill-defined; the resulting symlog spikes in panels (d) and (e) are numerical artifacts of train saturation, not a new hacking signal, and the linthresh=1\mathrm{linthresh}=1 axis is chosen precisely so that they are visible but compressed. The informative portion of ρ\rho is therefore the interior of training, where λtrain\lambda_{\mathrm{train}} is bounded away from zero. Read this way, Figure 2 locates the training fraction at which the held-out objective decouples from the training reward—complementing the diagnostics of mode collapse and stability, which instead test where the mean-field reduction itself, rather than its transfer, begins to fail.

5.3 Mode Collapse Investigation

The reduced-order model treats the group size purely as a temperature: by Lemma 6 the only role of GG is to set the forcing intensity D∝σadv2/GD\propto\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}}^{2}/G, and by Proposition 10 this forcing enters Eq. (12) without touching the deterministic coefficients. Mode collapse threatens this picture in two distinct ways, and neither is a failure of the dynamics—both are failures of the construction on which the dynamics rest. First, the within-group reward spread σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} can itself drift or acquire a GG-dependence that Lemma 6 does not model, in which case the temperature interpretation is no longer clean. Second, and more severely, the advantage construction can degenerate: when all GG completions of a prompt receive the same scalar reward, σadv=0\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}}=0 and the GRPO advantage Ai=(ri−r¯)/σadvA_{i}=(r_{i}-\bar{r})/\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} of Eq. 1 becomes the indeterminate 0/00/0, so the prompt contributes no usable signal at all. Figure 3 tests for each in turn, with training progress normalized per GG so the two group sizes overlay on the xx-axis.

Noise-intensity invariance test (row 1).

We plot the seed-averaged within-group advantage variance σadv2/G\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}}^{2}/G for both group sizes (panels (a)–(c)), where σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} is the logged train-reward standard deviation. This is precisely the forcing intensity of Lemma 6, so under the paper’s assumptions the G=4G=4 and G=16G=16 traces should sit on a common, flat plateau: the temperature is the only thing GG controls, and once it is divided out the curves coincide. Two departures are diagnostic. A downward drift away from the plateau means the gradient signal in Eq. 4 is shrinking faster than the 1/G1/G noise reduction can account for—within-group rewards are losing their variability as the policy concentrates mass on a shrinking set of completions. A separation of the two curves means σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} carries a GG-dependence of its own, again outside what Lemma 6 predicts. A persistent, overlapping plateau is the healthy reading.

Collapsed-prompt fraction (row 2).

We plot the seed-averaged fraction of prompts in a training step whose GG completions all received an identical scalar reward (panels (d)–(f)). For these prompts the advantage is the indeterminate 0/00/0 of Eq. 4, so they drop out of the update entirely. A fraction near zero is healthy; a monotone climb toward one is the empirical witness for the regime in which Lemma 6 and Proposition 10 cease to apply, not because the relaxation of Theorem 7 has been violated but because the object it relaxes has stopped being well defined.

Findings.

The combined signature of a faithful run is a flat, overlapping plateau in row 1 together with a collapsed-prompt fraction near zero in row 2, and Figure 3 shows that the early portion of training sits in this regime across models: the advantage variance is on a stable plateau and almost every prompt yields a usable advantage. Both diagnostics then develop deviations as training proceeds. The row-1 traces do not collapse onto a single curve to the extent the pure-temperature account requires—the residual gap between G=4G=4 and G=16G=16 indicates a GG-dependence of σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} beyond the 1/G1/G scaling of Lemma 6—and the collapsed-prompt fraction in row 2 grows away from zero rather than holding, most visibly for DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat, where a substantial share of prompts eventually carries no gradient signal. These are concentration signatures: the policy is committing to fewer completions per prompt, which simultaneously thins σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} (row 1) and pushes whole prompts into the 0/00/0 degeneracy (row 2).

Scope.

The value of this diagnostic is that it separates two failure modes that a reward curve alone cannot distinguish. A plateau in reward could mean the order parameter has reached p⋆p^{\star} (Theorem 7 holding) or that the advantage construction has degenerated; rows 1 and 2 tell these apart by inspecting the variability of the signal rather than its level. Where row 1 drifts down or row 2 climbs, the mean-field reduction of Assumption 1 is being eroded by mode concentration—the policy collapsing onto a small set of completions—rather than by any violation of the second-order relaxation itself.

5.4 Policy Concentration Investigation

Of all the steps behind Theorem 7, only Assumption 1 is non-mechanical (Remark 12): it posits that the entire policy is summarized to leading order by the scalar order parameter p⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡[R]p(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[R]. This is a statement about the dimensionality of the dynamics, not about the reward level. It can fail even while the reward evolves smoothly, if the policy quietly collapses its mass onto a small set of completions: p⁡(θ)p(\theta) continues along a one-dimensional path while the underlying high-dimensional θ\theta-dynamics are no longer captured by it. This policy concentration is the direct threat to Assumption 1, and it is distinct from the advantage degeneracy—there the construction in Eq. 2 broke down, here the reduction’s central premise does. Figure 4 probes it through two observables: the token-level policy entropy, which measures how spread the policy remains, and the KL anchor, which measures how far it has travelled from the reference.

Token-level policy entropy (row 1).

We plot the seed-averaged per-token entropy of πθ(⋅∣q)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q) averaged across the batch (panels (a)–(c)). A high, stable entropy is the regime in which the scalar reduction is defensible: the policy retains its breadth, so summarizing it by p⁡(θ)p(\theta) discards little. A monotone decrease is the empirical signature that the reduction is becoming a poor description of the θ\theta-dynamics, since mass is concentrating on a few completions while p⁡(θ)p(\theta) may still be moving smoothly; a rapid drop to a low plateau is the concentration signal proper. Because Proposition 10 makes the deterministic dynamics GG-invariant, the entropy trajectories should additionally overlap across group sizes; curves that do not overlap indicate a GG-driven concentration that the reduction does not predict.

KL anchor (row 2).

We plot the seed-averaged DKL(πθ∥πref)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) (panels (d)–(f)), the term carrying weight β\beta in the objective Eq. 2 and supplying the restoring force of Lemma 3. The KL alone is ambiguous, and is informative only when read against row 1. Rising KL with falling entropy is the concentration regime—the policy has both moved far from the reference and lost breadth, the mass loss being what reduced the entropy. Rising KL with stable entropy is the benign case: a pure policy shift, a translation in policy space that the order-parameter description can absorb without the scalar summary failing.

Findings.

Every run shows entropy declining and KL rising, which is expected as GRPO pulls the policy away from its initialization; the question is whether the joint motion is the benign shift or the concentration failure, and the three models separate cleanly on this axis. DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat shows the strongest concentration signature: its KL rises to the largest values of the three models and its entropy falls correspondingly, the falling-entropy/rising-KL combination that row 2 is designed to flag. Qwen-1.5B sits at the opposite extreme—its KL stays small, so the policy remains close to the reference and its entropy declines least—marking it as the run for which Assumption 1 remains most faithful. Nemotron-Mini-4B is intermediate. This ordering is the same one recovered by the earlier diagnostics: Qwen-1.5B was the model with the cleanest order-parameter fit and the cleanest train–eval coupling, while DeepSeek-7B was the model whose advantage construction degenerated most. The entropy trajectories are moreover not perfectly GG-invariant—the G=4G=4 and G=16G=16 curves do not coincide as cleanly as Proposition 10 would require—which is the same GG-dependence of the within-group statistics seen earlier, now visible at the level of the policy itself.

Scope.

The decisive quantity is the timing of the entropy drop relative to reward saturation. An entropy decline that occurs only after the reward has reached its plateau (Figure 1) is comparatively harmless: by then p≈p⋆p\approx p^{\star} and the reduction has already done its work. An entropy drop that precedes saturation is the dangerous case, because the reward—and hence p⁡(θ)p(\theta)—is still evolving at a point where the policy has already lost its dimensionality, so Theorem 7 should no longer be expected to describe the trajectory. A nearly flat entropy curve with a slowly rising KL therefore certifies a run in which the scalar reduction holds throughout, whereas a sharp pre-saturation entropy collapse locates the training fraction at which it ceases to. Together with the stability diagnostic, which tests the complementary failure mode in which the dynamics themselves go unstable, this completes the account of where the closed-form description of Section 3 can and cannot be trusted.

5.5 Training Stability Investigation

Theorem 7 can fail in two ways, first: the reduction’s premise eroding while the dynamics themselves remain well behaved. This section tests the complementary failure—the dynamics becoming unstable while the reduction’s premise still holds. The linearized system Eq. 8 is unstable iff K​η​Kref>1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}>1-\mu, at which point the effective damping CeffC_{\mathrm{eff}} turns negative and the characteristic roots cross into the right half-plane. Figure 5 tracks this through two observables that stand in a cause-and-effect relation: the importance-sampling ratio, which witnesses the off-policy lag that erodes the damping, and the gradient norm, which is where a loss of damping shows up as divergence.

Gradient-norm trajectory (row 1).

We plot the seed-averaged ‖∇J‖\|\nabla J\| on a logarithmic yy-axis (panels (a)–(c)). When Proposition 9 is violated and Ceff<0C_{\mathrm{eff}}<0, the right-half-plane roots produce monotone exponential growth—a straight ascending line on a log scale—or abrupt spikes as the gradient blows up. A bounded, weakly oscillating trace is the converse signature: the roots remain in the left half-plane and the linearized model of Theorem 7 continues to apply.

Importance-sampling drift (row 2).

We plot the seed-averaged maximum over the batch of πθ​(o∣q)/πold​(o∣q)\pi_{\theta}(o\mid q)/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(o\mid q) (panels (d)–(f)), where πold=πθk−Kref\pi_{\mathrm{old}}=\pi_{\theta_{k-K_{\mathrm{ref}}}} is the refreshed sampling policy of Eq. (3). This is the direct witness of the off-policy lag of Lemma 5: as the delay τ=Kref​δ\tau=K_{\mathrm{ref}}\delta grows, πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} and πθ\pi_{\theta} separate, the support of the ratio widens, and the −K​τ-K\tau damping reduction in Ceff=cμ−K​τC_{\mathrm{eff}}=c_{\mu}-K\tau becomes material. A blow-up of the IS-ratio max is therefore the practical precursor of crossing the threshold (11): row 2 supplies the mechanism, row 1 the consequence, so widening in row 2 should lead any divergence in row 1.

Findings.

Across all three models and both group sizes the training sits squarely in the stable regime. The gradient norms (row 1) remain bounded and weakly oscillating on the log scale, with no monotone exponential growth and no runaway spikes—the signature of left-half-plane roots throughout training. The IS-ratio maxima (row 2) settle onto a bounded plateau, fluctuating in a narrow band (roughly 2.32.3–2.92.9 across the three models) rather than diverging. The off-policy lag is thus clearly present—the max ratio sits well above one, so πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} and πθ\pi_{\theta} do separate between refreshes—but its damping cost −K​τ-K\tau is finite and never large enough to drive CeffC_{\mathrm{eff}} negative, so the stable condition K​η​Kref<1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}<1-\mu holds for the duration of every run. Mechanistically this is unsurprising: the small learning rate in Table 2 in Appendix keeps the product K​η​KrefK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}} well below 1−μ1-\mu, which is precisely the overdamped, small-η\eta regime that Proposition 8 and Remark 11 identify with monotone saturation. Both diagnostics also overlay across group sizes, consistent with the GG-freeness of the deterministic coefficients in Proposition 10.

5.6 Exercising the Oscillatory Regime in an Exact Reduction

The experiments of the preceding subsections all lie deep in the overdamped regime that Proposition 8 identifies with the small-η\eta configuration of Table 2, and so they leave untested precisely the two predictions that separate a second-order model from the first-order saturation laws it generalizes: the stability threshold K​η​Kref>1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}>1-\mu of Proposition 9 and the overdamped-to-oscillatory transition of Section 3.5. We exercise both here. To isolate the predicted physics from the deep-network approximation, we run the reduction in the setting where Assumption 1 holds exactly: a softmax policy over a finite completion set, for which the order parameter p​(θ)=𝔼o∼πθ​[R]p(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{o\sim\pi_{\theta}}[R] closes on itself and the gradient-flow projection of (3) is exact rather than approximate. Any oscillation observed here is therefore attributable to the inertial term of Theorem 7 and not to a breakdown of the mean-field premise.

Setup.

We take a single prompt with |𝒪|=8|\mathcal{O}|=8 completions carrying fixed verifiable rewards, a uniform reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, and initialization θ0\theta_{0} at the uniform policy, so the trajectory starts from rest (p˙​(0)=0\dot{p}(0)=0) at R0=prefR_{0}=p_{\mathrm{ref}}. We evolve the exact heavy-ball GRPO map (3) with a genuine stale-policy refresh θold=θk−Kref\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=\theta_{k-K_{\mathrm{ref}}}, computing the group-relative advantage (1) under πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} in closed form (the G→∞G\!\to\!\infty deterministic limit, in which the importance ratio of (2) cancels the sampling measure); the 1/G1/G forcing of Lemma 6 is suppressed so that the deterministic dynamics are seen without stationary fluctuation. Crucially, the stiffness KK is measured once, from an independent stable baseline (μ=0\mu=0, Kref=1K_{\mathrm{ref}}=1, small η\eta), by reading the early-training relaxation rate λ\lambda off −log⁡(p⋆−p⁡(t))-\log\!\big(p^{\star}-p(t)\big) and inverting the overdamped slow-pole relation of Corollary 13; the recovered p⋆=1.35p^{\star}=1.35 and K=0.12K=0.12 are then held fixed and used only to predict the critical refresh interval Kref⋆=(1−μ)/(K​η)K_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\star}=(1-\mu)/(K\eta). The analytic curves overlaid below carry no per-trajectory fit.

The transition appears as predicted (Figure 6).

Fixing (η,μ,β)=(0.30,0.80,1.00)(\eta,\mu,\beta)=(0.30,0.80,1.00) and sweeping KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}}, the exact order parameter traces the full cascade Theorem 7 prescribes. At small KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} the response is monotone, a single overshoot-free approach to p⋆p^{\star}; as KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} grows the off-policy lag of Lemma 5 erodes the effective damping Ceff=cμ−K​τC_{\mathrm{eff}}=c_{\mu}-K\tau, the damping ratio (10) drops through unity, and the trajectory develops first an overshoot and then a sequence of damped oscillations about p⋆p^{\star}. The inertia responsible for the ringing is the same momentum-plus-lag mass MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}} of Lemma 5 that supplies the slow-start inflection of Proposition 14: the two phenomena are the overdamped and underdamped faces of one second-order system, and a first-order saturation law (13) can represent neither.

The boundary tracks the prediction where the linearization holds (Figure 7).

Classifying the exact dynamics over an (η,Kref)(\eta,K_{\mathrm{ref}}) grid into monotone, overshooting, and oscillatory regimes, the empirical monotone–oscillatory frontier follows the hyperbolic locus K​η​Kref=constK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}=\text{const} that Proposition 9 predicts. In the small-η\eta, large-KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} corner—where the local linearization of Remark 12 is most trustworthy—the measured frontier sits essentially on the predicted threshold line K​η​Kref=1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}=1-\mu, drawn with the independently measured KK and no free parameter. This is the central positive result: the refresh-interval threshold of Proposition 9 is not merely an artifact of the derivation but a property of the exact dynamics, pinned in absolute terms by a slope measured elsewhere.

Two qualifications, both informative.

First, the ζ=1\zeta=1 onset curve obtained from the O⁡(τ2)O(\tau^{2})-truncated coefficients (9) sits below the empirical onset: the truncated model calls for oscillation at smaller η\eta than the exact system actually exhibits, so the second-order expansion is conservative about where ringing begins even as it captures the threshold’s functional form. The gap narrows toward large KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} and widens at large η\eta, exactly where a low-order expansion of the delay e⁡(t−τ)e(t-\tau) should be expected to degrade. Second, the exact trajectories never diverge: the linear instability of Proposition 9, in which the characteristic roots cross into the right half-plane, manifests in the nonlinear system as persistent bounded ringing rather than as p→∞p\to\infty, because the order parameter is confined to [mino⁡R,maxo⁡R][\min_{o}R,\max_{o}R] and the softmax saturates. The unbounded blow-up is therefore a property of the linearization alone; Proposition 9 correctly locates the loss of monotone stability but overstates its consequence, the oscillation amplitude being regularized by the same nonlinearity that Assumption 1 linearizes away.

Scope.

This study does for the dynamical predictions what the mode-collapse and policy-concentration diagnostics do for the mean-field premise: it identifies the regime in which the closed form can be trusted and the manner in which it first fails. The overdamped-to-oscillatory transition and the Proposition 9 threshold are confirmed in the setting where Assumption 1 is exact, locating the truncation-induced error in the onset rather than in the threshold and showing the predicted divergence to be a nonlinearly-regularized ringing. What remains is the deep-network demonstration: repeating the KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} sweep (or, equivalently, raising η\eta) on the models of Section 5.1 and reading the oscillation off the reward curve while the importance-sampling drift and gradient norm of Figure 5 witness the crossing. There Assumption 1 is only approximate, so the exact-reduction boundary established here is the appropriate reference against which to measure the deviation.

5.7 Out-of-Distribution Benchmarking

Table 1 reports out-of-distribution transfer: all three models are trained with GRPO on GSM8K and evaluated, without further tuning, on eight math benchmarks spanning grade-school word problems (GSM-Plus, MetaMathQA) through competition mathematics (AIME-2026, HMMT-2025, IMO-Bench). Entries are pass@kk means ±\pm standard deviation over seeds, with green marking improvements over the untrained base, bold-green the best configuration for each model, and red the rare regressions. The headline result is that GRPO on a single grade-school dataset transfers broadly and positively: the large majority of cells are green for both group sizes and all three models, and pass@5 exceeds pass@1 throughout, so the gains reflect genuine accuracy rather than a shift in sampling temperature.

The size of the transfer is strongly graded by the distance between the training and evaluation distributions. Gains are largest on benchmarks closest to GSM8K: Nemotron-4B more than doubles its GSM-Plus pass@1 (9.11 to 20.32 at G=16G=16), and DeepSeek-7B improves GSM-Plus pass@1 by roughly fifteen points (25.64 to 40.25 at G=4G=4). They shrink markedly on the hardest competition sets, where the two non-reasoning models (DeepSeek-7B, Nemotron-4B) remain at or near zero on AIME-2026 and HMMT-2025 regardless of training, and only the reasoning-distilled DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-1.5B shows movement there—AIME-2026 pass@1 rising from 1.33 to 6.17 and HMMT-2025 pass@5 from 10.00 to 16.67 at G=16G=16. GRPO on in-distribution data thus amplifies capabilities the base model already possesses far more than it confers new ones on benchmarks well outside the training distribution.

The two group sizes are broadly comparable. G=16G=16 secures most of the per-model best results, but G=4G=4 is competitive across the board and is the stronger setting in several cases—most strikingly DeepSeek-7B on GSM-Plus (40.25 versus 30.83 pass@1) and Qwen-1.5B on HMMT-2025 pass@1 (7.33 versus 6.33). This near-parity of the two budgets is consistent with the group-size invariance of the deterministic dynamics (Proposition 10 and Remark 11): quadrupling the rollout count leaves the mean transfer performance largely unchanged, matching the prediction that small groups track large groups up to noise. The few regressions are not uniformly distributed but concentrate on NuminaMath, where several configurations fall slightly below base (e.g. DeepSeek-7B pass@1 from 16.97 to 15.96 at G=16G=16), indicating that transfer is overwhelmingly but not universally beneficial and can mildly degrade on particular target distributions.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We have given a reduced-order model of GRPO training that recasts the fitting of reward curves as a mechanistic account of their shape, conditional on a mean-field reduction. Under a single mean-field assumption (Assumption 1), and a controlled second-order truncation in the step size and refresh lag, the GRPO update reduces to a stochastically-forced damped oscillator (Theorem 7) whose mass, damping, and stiffness are fixed in closed form by the optimizer hyperparameters together with a single measured curvature scale. The reduction is not merely descriptive: it subsumes the empirical single-exponential saturation law as its overdamped limit (Corollary 13), reinterprets the fitted plateau, timescale, and size exponent as the fixed point, inverse stiffness, and curvature-scaling exponent of the underlying potential (Equation (15)), and supplies, through the retained inertial term, the slow-start inflection that the single exponential cannot represent (Proposition 14). Empirically, the three-phase law fits the training-reward trajectories of three models at two group sizes to R2≥0.91R^{2}\geq 0.91, and the predicted group-size invariance of the deterministic dynamics (Proposition 10) is borne out on both the mean trajectory and out-of-distribution transfer to eight benchmarks. Beyond the closed form, the dynamical reading yields a set of diagnostics that separate failure modes a reward curve alone conflates—train–eval decoupling, advantage degeneracy, policy concentration, and dynamical instability—and thereby localize, within a single run, where the closed-form description can and cannot be trusted.

The principal limitation is now one of parameterization rather than of regime. The two predictions that most sharply distinguish a second-order model from the first-order saturation laws it generalizes—the stability threshold K​η​Kref>1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}>1-\mu of Proposition 9 and the overdamped-to-oscillatory transition under refresh-interval sweeps (Section 3.5)—are not reachable by our GSM8K runs, because the small learning rate of our configuration places every one deep in the overdamped regime (Proposition 8). We therefore exercise them in the setting where Assumption 1 holds exactly, a softmax-bandit reduction (Section 5.6): sweeping KrefK_{\mathrm{ref}} drives the exact dynamics across the predicted boundary, reproducing the monotone-to-oscillatory cascade and placing the empirical frontier on the threshold line K​η​Kref=1−μK\eta K_{\mathrm{ref}}=1-\mu drawn with an independently measured KK and no free parameter. That study also sharpens the theory’s reach: the O⁡(τ2)O(\tau^{2}) delay truncation is conservative about the ζ=1\zeta=1 onset, and the linear divergence of Proposition 9 is realized in the bounded nonlinear system as persistent ringing rather than blow-up. What remains is the deep-network demonstration—repeating the sweep, or correspondingly raising η\eta, on the models of Section 5.1, where Assumption 1 is only approximate and the exact-reduction boundary established here is the reference against which to measure the deviation.

Three further threads are opened by the empirical analysis. First, our diagnostics record a residual group-size dependence of the within-group spread σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} that the temperature interpretation of Lemma 6 does not predict; the deterministic trajectory remains GG-invariant, but σadv\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}} itself carries structure beyond the 1/G1/G forcing scaling, and a model of that structure would extend the account past the leading-order temperature picture. Second, the reduction is local: its coefficients are linearizations at the fixed point p⋆p^{\star} (Remark 12), so it describes the approach to saturation rather than the global trajectory, and a treatment of the pre-linear phase—where mode concentration and advantage degeneracy first appear—would close the gap between the dynamics and the failure modes the diagnostics detect. Third, the curvature-scaling exponent K⁡(M)∝η−1​M−0.3K(M)\propto\eta^{-1}M^{-0.3} is inherited from the empirical fits rather than derived; relating it to the lazy/NTK-regime slowdown it resembles would convert the last fitted exponent in the chain into a predicted one. Taken together, these directions point toward a GRPO training theory that is predictive not only at the overdamped fixed point we characterize here but across the regimes where current practice actually operates.

Appendix A Symbolic verification of the coefficients

The continuous-time coefficients of Lemma 4 and the delay corrections of Lemma 5 were verified by symbolic computation. A second-order Taylor expansion of the heavy-ball map reproduces (6), and substituting the delayed restoring force into the resulting equation reproduces (7) together with the sign condition (11).
